clinicalPearls: A rare neonatal deformity in which the knee is hyperextended at birth, ranging along a spectrum from simple recurvatum through anterior subluxation to frank dislocation of the tibia on the femur
The severity is graded clinically and radiographically by the degree of anterior tibial displacement and by how much passive flexion can be achieved

It is strongly associated with other packaging and connective-tissue conditions, notably developmental dysplasia of the hip, clubfoot, arthrogryposis, and Larsen syndrome, so a full musculoskeletal and syndromic assessment is essential
Contracture and fibrosis of the quadriceps with a tight anterior capsule prevent flexion and maintain the deformity
Early treatment, ideally begun in the neonatal period, uses gentle serial casting or splinting to progressively flex the knee while the tissues are most compliant
The frequent coexistence of hip dysplasia means treatment must be coordinated, as knee extension casting can conflict with the flexion-abduction positioning used for the hip
Irreducible or resistant dislocations, or those in syndromic children, may require surgical quadriceps lengthening and capsular release
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital dislocation of the knee is characterised by fixed hyperextension due to contracture of the quadriceps mechanism and anterior knee capsule, so that the tibia is displaced or dislocated anteriorly on the femur. The quadriceps is often fibrotic and foreshortened, the cruciate ligaments may be hypoplastic or absent, and the suprapatellar pouch is obliterated, all of which resist flexion. It may occur in isolation as a packaging phenomenon from abnormal intrauterine position, particularly with breech presentation and oligohydramnios, or as part of a generalised condition such as arthrogryposis or Larsen syndrome in which multiple joints are affected by connective-tissue laxity or contracture.
additionalDifferentials: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita with knee involvement
Larsen syndrome with multiple congenital dislocations
Developmental dysplasia of the hip presenting as part of the same spectrum
Neuromuscular knee deformity such as that in myelomeningocele
additionalInvestigations: Clinical grading of the deformity and the achievable range of passive flexion
Lateral knee radiographs to assess anterior tibial displacement and grade the dislocation
Ultrasound or radiography of the hips to exclude coexisting dysplasia
Examination for clubfoot and other associated deformities
Assessment for arthrogryposis, Larsen syndrome, or other syndromic features
Genetic evaluation where a syndrome is suspected
redFlags: An irreducible knee that cannot be brought into flexion with gentle manipulation
Features of arthrogryposis, Larsen syndrome, or another generalised connective-tissue disorder
Coexisting hip dislocation or clubfoot requiring coordinated management
Skin compromise or neurovascular concern from severe hyperextension
Failure to respond to early conservative treatment
reference.prognosis: Isolated, reducible dislocations treated early with serial casting generally achieve a stable, functional, well-flexing knee, whereas irreducible or syndromic cases have a more guarded outlook and often require surgery and prolonged rehabilitation.
pitfalls: Failing to begin gentle correction in the neonatal period when the tissues are most amenable
Overlooking coexisting hip dysplasia, or managing the hip and knee positioning in conflict
Missing an underlying syndrome such as arthrogryposis or Larsen syndrome
Applying forceful manipulation that risks physeal or growth-plate injury
Underestimating the need for surgery in resistant or syndromic dislocations
management: Begin gentle serial casting or splinting in progressive flexion in the neonatal period while the tissues remain compliant
Coordinate positioning with concurrent hip dysplasia treatment, as knee-extension casting conflicts with the flexion-abduction posture used for the hip
Surgical quadriceps lengthening with V-Y quadricepsplasty and anterior capsular release for irreducible or resistant dislocations
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation to restore flexion and quadriceps function after reduction
Screen for and manage associated developmental hip dysplasia, clubfoot and other packaging deformities
Assess for arthrogryposis or Larsen syndrome with genetic evaluation where syndromic features are present
Paediatric orthopaedic follow-up to monitor knee stability and function through growth
